title: How to balance global benefits consistency with local relevance
summary: What to keep the same in every country, what to adapt locally and how to keep a global benefits strategy fair when packages differ.
body_markdown:
*This article was first published by*[REBA](https://reba.global/resource/how-to-balance-global-benefits-consistency-with-local-relevance.html) *.*


‍


When a company grows into new countries, its benefits rarely grow evenly. Head office usually has the full package. A newer office might have private medical and not much else, and people there notice. More global employers are setting out to fix that.[70% had a global minimum standard for benefits](https://www.wtwco.com/en-gb/news/2024/01/almost-three-quarters-of-employers-have-set-a-global-minimum-standard-for-employee-benefits) by the end of 2023, almost double the share in 2019.


It might seem like one package for everyone is the obvious answer. But tax rules, state healthcare and local markets mean the same benefit can be worth a lot in one country and little in the next.


Instead, a global benefits strategy works best with a consistent core. Your principles, minimum standards and the way people access benefits stay the same everywhere. Then each country picks the benefits that work best locally.


Here's what to keep consistent, what to adapt, how to judge fairness and how to roll it out.


## What should be consistent in a global benefits strategy?


These four things should be the same in every country:


- **Why you offer benefits.** A clear benefits philosophy sets out what your benefits are for, like protecting health, supporting families or helping you hire. When a country wants to add something, you can check whether it fits.
- **A minimum standard.** Decide the minimum every employee should get. Think in outcomes, such as life cover worth twice salary or weeks of paid parental leave, so each country can meet it in its own way.
- **Access to benefits.** Someone in your smallest office should see what they're entitled to as easily as someone at head office.
- **Who decides what.** Agree which decisions are made centrally and which are made in each country.[Only 25% of global benefits leaders](https://aon.mediaroom.com/2025-07-29-Companies-Struggle-to-Meet-Rising-Demand-for-Personalized-Benefits,-Aon-Survey-Finds) say their governance supports their goals.


## What should change from country to country?


Usually the benefits themselves should change.


Tax is the first reason. A wellness budget that's tax efficient in one country can be taxed as pay in another, so people there get less from the same spend.


What the state provides matters too. If public healthcare covers something well, your money goes further on something it doesn't. Salary sacrifice and flexible benefits are common in the UK, while in some countries there's little on offer beyond basic insurance.


If a local provider works well and employees know it, keep it. A global strategy doesn't mean using the same provider everywhere. Happl works with your existing brokers and providers, so local arrangements can stay in place.


## How do you keep benefits fair when they differ by country?


Fairness is about equal value, not identical benefits.


Healthcare is a good example. In the US, employer health insurance is the main way working people get cover at all. In the UK, private medical insurance sits on top of the NHS and can mean people get treated faster. The offerings aren't identical, but both make healthcare easier to access.


When you compare countries, count what people already get by law or local custom, because some start from a much higher base. Employees in Belgium often get meal vouchers, and in Brazil and the Philippines a 13th-month salary is mandatory. So adding the same benefit in every country won't leave everyone equally well off.


Then look at what each country's package is worth and who's using it, not just what's listed. A benefit few people use isn't adding much, however good it looks on paper.


## How to roll out a global benefits strategy in stages


Start by mapping what's offered in each country, who's eligible, what it costs and who runs it. The countries furthest from your minimum standard will stand out.


Work out what meeting the standard would cost in each country. Then bring those countries up first and work through the rest.


Make sure you have the systems and technology to scale it. They should apply each country's rules from one setup and show employees only what they're eligible for. And they should let you compare cost and take-up across countries.


[Happl](https://happl.com/) is the benefits operating system for global benefits, covering more than 160 countries. Eligibility and local tax rules are set per country in one place, so each employee sees only the benefits they qualify for. And you can see cost and take-up across every country side by side.


## Balancing global consistency with local relevance


You don't have to choose between consistency and local relevance. Keep the principles, the minimum standard and the way people access benefits the same everywhere. Let the benefits themselves follow local tax, healthcare and markets. That way employees in every country get a package that's fair and fits where they live, and your team can still run it as one strategy.
